title: GitHub Introduces Default "Cooldown" Policy for Dependabot Version Updates
gist: GitHub has made Dependabot wait three days before opening pull requests for non-security dependency updates, treating automated upgrade speed itself as the supply-chain attack surface after an incident where compromised packages downloaded 2 billion times a week stayed live on npm for about two hours. The cooldown is configurable, exempts security fixes, and is explicitly framed as one layer among lockfiles, disabled install scripts, and scoped CI tokens.

insights.claim: GitHub's Dependabot now waits at least three days after a new non-security dependency release is published before opening an upgrade pull request, changing the default from immediate to delayed.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Shifts the default cadence of automated dependency upgrades across millions of repos; package publishers lose the instant-adoption channel.
insights.locator: Instead of immediately opening pull requests

insights.claim: The three-day cooldown is configurable per-repository through the cooldown option in dependabot.yml rather than being a hard-coded platform rule.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Teams can tune exposure vs. patch latency; enterprises with stricter policies are not forced onto GitHub's default.
insights.locator: This behavior is configurable through the cooldown option

insights.claim: Security updates are explicitly exempt from the cooldown, so fixes for publicly known vulnerabilities still ship without delay.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The policy trades latency only on feature upgrades, not on CVE remediation - so mean-time-to-patch metrics should not regress.
insights.locator: The cooldown does not apply to security updates

insights.claim: GitHub product manager Carlin Cherry frames three days as an emerging community consensus rather than a GitHub-specific choice, positioning the default as cross-tool consistency.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Signals convergence across dependency-bot vendors; expect Renovate-class tools and registries to standardize on similar windows.
insights.quote: so this default behavior keeps Dependabot consistent as developers move between tools
insights.locator: Cherry notes that a three-day delay is emerging

insights.claim: A past dependency-poisoning incident compromised packages collectively downloaded more than 2 billion times a week, and the malicious versions stayed live on npm for roughly two hours.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Quantifies the exposure window automation must survive: two hours of registry availability was enough to industrialize the blast radius.
insights.quote: more than enough time for an automated update tool to see the new version, open a pull request, and put it in front of your team
insights.locator: GitHub product manager Carlin Cherry explains

insights.claim: Automated update tooling is itself the delivery mechanism for a growing share of supply chain attacks, because malicious code enters build pipelines within minutes of publication and before any human or scanner reviews it.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Automation speed is the attack surface; security spend should target ingestion latency, not just scanning coverage.
insights.quote: The malicious code rides in on a brand-new release, is published to a public registry, and gets pulled into build pipelines within minutes, before a human or a scanner has even looked at it.

insights.claim: The cooldown only defends against the fast-moving publish-and-propagate case and must be paired with lockfile pinning, disabled install scripts in CI, scoped build-pipeline tokens, and pre-merge review.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A checklist for auditing a portfolio company's build pipeline; cooldown alone is a partial control that can create false confidence.
insights.quote: pinning dependencies with lockfiles, disabling install scripts in CI where you can, scoping the tokens in your build pipelines, and reviewing updates before they merge
insights.locator: Because a cooldown only addresses the fast-moving case

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter argued cooldowns could become self-defeating if universal adoption means fewer early adopters remain to encounter and report malicious packages.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A herd-immunity critique worth tracking: if delay windows converge industry-wide, detection may depend entirely on paid scanning vendors.
insights.quote: if everyone will be delaying updates
insights.locator: On Hacker News, commenter zihotki questioned

insights.claim: The counter-argument is that cooldown security relies on dedicated security-scanning parties finding malicious releases, not on ordinary users being victimized first, so universal delay does not degrade detection.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: If correct, value accrues to automated registry-scanning vendors rather than to community reporting - a tailwind for software supply chain security tooling.
insights.quote: the security assumption behind cooldowns rests on security scanning parties, not on innocent users being victimized

insights.claim: Practitioner feedback holds that most dodgy releases get publicly flagged on GitHub or Reddit within a day or two, so a three-day window also catches ordinary breakage, not just malice.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Reliability benefit is a second, under-priced justification for cooldowns beyond security - reduces CI breakage from bad releases.
insights.quote: Three days feels about right for catching the worst breakage before it hits your CI.
